title: The Two Kinds of Difficulty and Ease in Practice
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: (Original text excerpted from *Master Xuyun's Convenient Teachings*)

inline.s: (Original text excerpted from *Master Xuyun's Convenient Teachings*)

For those who devote themselves to practice, according to the depth of their skill, there are two kinds of difficulty and ease: first, the difficulty and ease of the beginner; second, the difficulty and ease of the seasoned practitioner.

blocks.text: 1. The Difficulty and Ease of the Beginner
1. The Beginner's Difficulty — The Thieving Mind Does Not Die

inline.s: [Thieving mind] The grasping mind. Because the grasping mind steals the Dharma-wealth, preventing the true Dharma from appearing, the Chan communities call it the thieving mind. The *Collection of Pressing Black Beans* (Ǎn Hēi Dòu Jí) says:
“If the thieving mind does not die, it is the student's great affliction.”

[Grasping mind] The mind that arises by grasping the six sense-objects, also called the conditioned mind. [Dharma-wealth] The counterpart of “worldly wealth,” referring to the Buddhadharma. Because the Buddhadharma nourishes living beings and is the provision that nurtures their wisdom-life, just as worldly treasures do, it is metaphorically called Dharma-wealth.

The common ailment of the beginner is that deluded thoughts and ingrained habits cannot be put down; ignorance and arrogance, jealousy and obstruction, greed, anger, delusion, and craving, laziness and gluttony, and all the disputes of self and others swell up and fill the belly to bursting — how could such a person ever be in accord with the Way?
[Arrogance (gòng gāo)] Pride and conceit.

Some come from pampered, well-to-do backgrounds and cannot shake off their old habits; they cannot bear the slightest grievance or endure the least hardship — how could they apply themselves to practice? They never stop to think what kind of person our root teacher Śākyamuni Buddha was when he left home.
Some who know a few written characters do not realize that the questions in the records of the ancient worthies were meant to test the depth of the student,
(that is, to examine the depth of the student's practice)

; instead they pride themselves on being clever, and spend their days chasing words and phrases, talking of the mind and of the Buddha, and taking the ancients' sayings as intellectual explanations. Engaging in the business of describing food and counting others' treasures, they still think highly of themselves and give rise to great arrogance. When they meet a serious illness, they cry out in misery; or when the thirtieth of the twelfth month arrives
(that is, when death arrives)
, they are thrown into confusion; all their lifetime of intellectual understanding is of no use whatsoever, and only then do they regret it, but it is too late.

There is yet another kind of person who misconstrues the saying, “You are originally a Buddha, beyond cultivation and realization.” They claim that since it is inherently complete and ready-made, there is no need to cultivate or realize, and so they idle their days away, indulging their whims in lax self-indulgence. Wasting their time, they even call themselves “people beyond convention, at ease with conditions.” Such people are about to suffer a great deal.
Those with a little aspiration for the Way, on the other hand, cannot find a place to begin.
Some are afraid of deluded thoughts; unable to get rid of them, they are vexed all day long, blaming themselves for their heavy karmic obstructions, and so their aspiration for the Way recedes.

Some want to fight the deluded thoughts to the death: indignantly clenching their fists, puffing up their chests, glaring wide-eyed, they make a great show of it, as if determined to wage a life-and-death battle with their thoughts. Little do they know that thoughts cannot be fought off this way — they only end up spitting blood or going mad.
Some are afraid of falling into emptiness; little do they know that a “ghost” has already been born, so that they can neither empty out the emptiness nor awaken to anything.
Some use the mind to seek awakening; little do they know that seeking awakening and wanting to become a Buddha are themselves a great delusion. Sand is not the source of rice
(boiled sand can never become rice)
, and even if they seek until the “year of the donkey” (a year that never comes), they will certainly never awaken.

Some happen upon a stick or two of quiet incense, and their hearts leap with joy; but that is merely a blind turtle happening upon a hole in a floating log — a chance encounter, not genuine skill; and so they add yet another layer of obstruction, the obstruction of joy.
[A stick or two of quiet incense] During those one or two sticks of incense, the mind is clear and still.
Some find that in stillness the mind feels clear and pleasant, but in activity it no longer works, and so they shun the bustling world for quiet, passing their days sitting in dead water.
Cases like these are many, very many.
For the beginner who cannot find the path, practice is truly difficult: with awareness but no illumination, one's scattered mind cannot “settle on the seat”
(that is, the mind is scattered and the practice cannot settle)
; with illumination but no awareness, one sits soaking in dead water.

blocks.text: 2. The Beginner's Ease — Put It Down and Raise a Single Thought

inline.s: Though practice is said to be difficult, once you find the path it is also very easy. What is the beginner's ease? There is no trick to it — just put it down. Put down what? Put down all ignorance and affliction.

Fellow practitioners! This bodily shell of ours — once the breath stops, it is nothing but a corpse. The reason we cannot put things down is only that we treasure it; from that arise self and other, right and wrong, love and hate, grasping and rejecting. If you firmly regard this shell as a corpse, do not cherish it, and at root do not take it to be “me,” then what is there left that you cannot put down?

As long as you can put it down, then at all times and places — whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, in stillness or in activity, at leisure or busy — your whole body, inside and out, will be cool and composed, holding only a single doubt; keep doubting on evenly and unceasingly, without mixing in the slightest extraneous thought. A single huatou is like a heaven-leaning sword: whatever touches its edge is wiped out without trace. What deluded thoughts need you fear? What idle person can disturb you? Who is there to distinguish stillness from activity? Who is there to cling to existence or to emptiness?

If you fear deluded thoughts, you add yet another deluded thought; the moment you feel “pure,” it is no longer purity; the moment you fear falling into emptiness, you have already fallen into existence; the moment you want to become a Buddha, you have already entered the path of demons.
Therefore, as long as you recognize the path
(the path is this one thought of putting everything down and raising only the huatou)

, then carrying water and hauling firewood are none other than the wondrous Way, and hoeing the fields and tilling the land are all occasions of Chan. It is not only when you sit cross-legged in meditation all day that you count as practicing the Way.

blocks.text: 2. The Difficulty and Ease of the Seasoned Practitioner
1. The Seasoned Practitioner's Difficulty — Unable to Advance Beyond the Top of a Hundred-Foot Pole

inline.s: What is the seasoned practitioner's difficulty? When the seasoned practitioner's practice reaches the point where genuine doubt appears before him, then with awareness and illumination he is still within birth and death, and without awareness and illumination he falls into blank extinction. At this stage it is truly difficult; many who reach it cannot break free, and stand at the top of the hundred-foot pole unable to advance a step.
[Genuine doubt] True doubt — investigating, thought after thought without interruption, back to before a single thought has arisen. (See
The Chan of Master Xuyun
.) [Standing at the top of a hundred-foot pole, unable to advance] Master Daoyuan
wrote in a verse
“A person unmoving at the top of a hundred-foot pole
not a single thought arises
, though he has gained entry, it is not yet true
not yet final
; from the top of the hundred-foot pole he must take another step
thoroughly seeing the fundamental nature
, and the worlds of the ten directions are his whole body.”
(from the *Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp*)
There are some
(that is, some people)

who, having reached this stage and gained a slight hold on their practice, and having met no state they could not break through, imagine that they have cut off ignorance completely and perfected their skill. Little do they know that they are passing their days sitting in the cave of ignorance without even realizing it. When they suddenly meet a state they cannot break through, they cannot be master of themselves, and are carried away by it as before — what a pity!

Others, having reached the stage where genuine doubt appears and a little wisdom has arisen in emptiness, and having grasped a few of the ancients' public cases, let go of the doubt and imagine they have achieved great, thorough awakening. They compose poems and verses, wink their eyes and raise their brows, and call themselves good spiritual teachers. Such people delude themselves and delude others, and their offense is boundless.

There are still others who misconstrue Bodhidharma's “Outwardly cease all conditions, inwardly the mind has no panting; the mind like a wall, one can enter the Way,” together with the Sixth Patriarch's “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just this very
nèn

moment, what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?” — mistaking the meaning, they take sitting beside the withered tree as the ultimate. Such people take the conjured city for the treasure house, and mistake a guest-house for their homeland. The old woman who burned the hermitage was scolding just such dead men.

[Mistaking the meaning] 1. In Bodhidharma's instruction, “Outwardly cease all conditions, inwardly the mind has no panting; the mind like a wall, one can enter the Way,” the phrase “one can enter the Way” means that one can begin to realize the Way; that is, once the first three lines are accomplished, the preparatory work for realization is done. Yet some people mistakenly think that accomplishing “outwardly cease all conditions, inwardly the mind has no panting, the mind like a wall” is itself realization, is itself the final truth. 2. In the Sixth Patriarch's instruction, “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just this very moment, what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?” the word “nǎge” means “which one” in modern Chinese (in the ancient language there was no character “nǎ”; the character “nà” had two senses, one the modern “nà” meaning “that,” the other the modern “nǎ” meaning “which”), and not the modern “nàge” meaning “that one.” Yet some people mistakenly take “nàge shì Míng shàngzuò běnlái miànmù” to mean, expressed in modern Chinese, “that (That) is your original face.” They therefore mistakenly think that “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just this very moment” is itself the original face.

[Conjured city] A magically conjured city. This is the parable of the conjured city in the *Lotus Sūtra*. The place where all living beings attain Buddhahood is the treasure house, but the road to this treasure house is long, steep, and distant. Fearing that travelers would grow weary and turn back, the Buddha conjured up a city midway so that they could rest for a while and recover their strength, and then press straight on to the treasure house. The Buddha wishes all living beings to realize Buddhahood, but because living beings are timid at heart and weak in strength, unable to bear the burden, he first taught the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle, so that they might attain this nirvāṇa as a temporary resting place, and from there further rouse the great resolve to advance toward the true treasure house of Mahāyāna nirvāṇa (Buddhahood).

[The old woman who burned the hermitage] A Chan public case: Long ago, an old woman supported a hermit for twenty years, always sending a young girl to bring him meals and wait on him. One day the old woman told the girl to embrace him and ask, “How do you feel right now?” The hermit said, “A withered tree leaning against a cold cliff — for three winters not a trace of warmth.” The girl reported these words to the old woman. The old woman said, “For twenty years I have only been supporting a worldly fellow (an unawakened ordinary person)!” So she drove him away and burned down the thatched hermitage. This case shows that the hermit took the conjured city for the treasure house (thinking that the state of a single thought not arising was the ultimate), able to die but not to live. (See the *Compendium of Five Lamps*.)

blocks.text: 2. The Seasoned Practitioner's Ease — Continue Densely and Unceasingly

inline.s: What is the seasoned practitioner's ease? At this point, as long as you are not complacent and do not break off, but continue on densely and unceasingly
(densely and unceasingly investigating back to before a single thought has arisen)
, becoming denser within the dense and finer within the fine, then when the time comes, the bottom of the bucket will drop out of itself
(illumining the mind and seeing the nature)
. If it is not so, go and seek a good spiritual teacher to pull out the nails and draw out the wedges.
[Pulling out nails and drawing out wedges] Releasing adhesions and removing bonds.

Master Hanshan sang in verse: “High on the mountain's topmost height, I gaze around — unbounded view; in stillness sitting, hid from sight, a lonely moon lights the cold spring's hue. Within the spring no moon is found, the moon is in the blue sky's round; I chant this one short lay, yet in the lay no Chan holds sway.”
The first two lines
(“High on the mountain's topmost height, I gaze around — unbounded view”)
say that the true and constant stands alone revealed, belonging to nothing, the whole earth shining bright without the slightest obstruction; the third line
(“In stillness sitting, hid from sight”)

says that ordinary people certainly cannot recognize the wondrous essence of thusness, and even the buddhas of the three times cannot find where I dwell — hence “known to none”; the three lines beginning with “A lonely moon lights the cold spring”
(the three lines “A lonely moon lights the cold spring's hue; within the spring no moon is found, the moon is in the blue sky's round”)
are the old master's skillful means of likening this state; the last two lines
(“I chant this one short lay, yet in the lay no Chan holds sway”)
warn us, lest people mistake the pointing finger for the moon — words and language are not Chan at all!

[Mistaking the pointing finger for the moon] Taking the finger that points at the moon for the moon itself. [Words and language are not Chan] The words and language that speak of Chan point toward Chan; they are not Chan itself.
